reception.text: A wire dispatch ran in the Los Angeles Herald under "PORTO RICO LANDS / President Makes First Reservation For Naval Purposes," and on page one of the San Bernardino Sun and the Bakersfield Morning Echo.
reception.source: Los Angeles Herald, San Bernardino Sun, Morning Echo, June 30, 1903 (California Digital Newspaper Collection)

reception.text: The Santa Barbara Weekly Press carried the same dispatch.
No editorial comment has been found, and searches of Colorado and New York papers found nothing on the reservation.

political_impact.text: The Presidio, San Juan's penitentiary, was withdrawn from the naval reservation four days after it was reserved.
Congress passed an act to readjust the boundaries of the naval reservations in Puerto Rico.
The governor and a Navy commodore exchanged deeds, and Proclamation 819 returned most of the 80-acre Caguas Road tract to the island, keeping the naval hospital and wireless station.

legacy.text: The Navy built nothing on Isla Grande until a naval air station contract was awarded on October 30, 1939; the site was largely mangrove swamp and tidal flats, and most of the station was built on dredged fill.
legacy.source: Bureau of Yards and Docks, Building the Navy's Bases in World War II (1947), vol. 2, ch. 18

legacy.text: The Navy and Marines used Culebra for advance-base and landing exercises in the 1910s and 1920s and as a gunnery and bombing range from the late 1930s.
Senator Edmund Muskie entered press accounts into the Congressional Record reporting that 304 of 313 Culebra families had asked the Navy to leave; protest and civil disobedience followed in 1971.
Navy training on Culebra ended, with operations moving to Vieques.

today.name: Fernando Luis Ribas Dominicci Airport (Isla Grande)
today.note: Isla Grande became a naval air station and later San Juan's Isla Grande Airport.

later_actions.text: Act of Congress readjusting the boundaries of the naval reservations in Puerto Rico.
Executive Order 8684 added a naval defensive sea area at Culebra.
Former Navy lands on Culebra were divided between the Commonwealth and the Fish and Wildlife Service.

uncertain: No departmental request has been found for the San Juan harbor parcels reserved to the Navy.
When Isla Grande passed to civil airport use is not documented in the sources consulted.

reception.text: The Los Angeles Herald ran a short item headed "Land Reservations in Porto Rico"; whether it reported this proclamation or the Presidio order is not known.

political_impact.text: Customs at San Juan got only the use, "until otherwise ordered," of buildings on Puntilla Point, which had just been reserved to the Navy.

legacy.text: The civilian reservations became the custom houses, Marine Hospital Service sites and light-house stations of federal Puerto Rico; several of the light stations named still stand.

related.note: Same-week reservation of property for the federal courts.

uncertain: Whether the Los Angeles Herald item of July 1, 1903 concerned this proclamation is not known.

political_impact.text: Withdrew the Presidio, San Juan's penitentiary, from the naval reservation made four days earlier; the order gives no reason.

related.note: Withdrew the Presidio from Proclamation 502's naval reservation.

uncertain: Who asked for the Presidio's withdrawal is not known; Governor Hunt's administration is a candidate but unconfirmed.

political_impact.text: Added no land; kept the President's right to amend the naval reservation and invited the Secretary of the Navy and the governor to set down how the lands would be used.
political_impact.source: Lord, Presidential Executive Orders, Numbered (1944), vol. 1, pp. 21–22

related.note: Conditioned the naval reservation of June 26, 1903.

legacy.text: Lands near Aibonito reserved for military purposes by this order were transferred to Puerto Rico in 1920.
legacy.source: EO 3310; Lord, Presidential Executive Orders, Numbered (1944), vol. 1, p. 281

later_actions.text: Executive Order 3310 transferred to Puerto Rico certain lands near Aibonito reserved by this order.
later_actions.source: Lord, Presidential Executive Orders, Numbered (1944), vol. 1, p. 281

political_impact.text: All federal land in Puerto Rico not reserved by the President before July 1, 1903 passed to the island government.
political_impact.source: Fourth Annual Report of the Governor of Porto Rico (1904), S. Doc. 35, 58th Cong., 3d sess.

political_impact.text: No organized objection to the reservations has been found; debate over Puerto Rico in these years concerned its political status, tariffs and citizenship.
